draft.exec:
Seoul Live Tickets lost 40 minutes of sales during a March on-sale, and scalper bots took seats from real fans. Moving off the current Singapore hosting to a cloud design that absorbs thirty-fold traffic jumps protects revenue and fan trust.

This proposal keeps your team on PostgreSQL while adding an order queue, edge caching and bot challenges so the site stays responsive when a K-pop tour goes on sale.

Approving a load test before the next major on-sale confirms the design handles your peak traffic.

needs.need: Site went down for 40 minutes during a big sale.
needs.quote: the site went down for 40 minutes during a big sale
needs.answer: An order queue holds purchase requests until workers save them, and compute scales out across two zones. This reduces the chance of another outage during on-sales.

needs.need: Bots buy up seats for scalpers.
needs.quote: Bots also buy up seats for scalpers
needs.answer: A challenge at login and checkout stops automated buyers, and edge filtering blocks known bot patterns. Real fans get fairer access to tickets.

needs.need: Traffic jumps about 30x in the first ten minutes.
needs.quote: traffic jumps about 30x in the first ten minutes
needs.answer: Compute capacity grows with demand and shrinks after the rush. You pay for extra capacity only during the on-sale window instead of running it all day.

needs.need: Team knows PostgreSQL and wants to keep using it.
needs.quote: We already use PostgreSQL and our team knows it well
needs.answer: The database layer runs PostgreSQL-compatible storage across two zones. Your team keeps their existing skills while gaining higher availability than the current setup.

outcomes.title: Revenue protected during flash sales
outcomes.text: Orders queue up instead of failing when fans rush in, and the database writes them steadily. Fewer dropped purchases means more tickets sold per on-sale.

outcomes.title: Cost follows the on-sale curve
outcomes.text: Baseline compute stays small between sales. Capacity rises only when fans arrive and falls back afterward, turning fixed hosting spend into variable cost tied to actual ticket demand.

outcomes.title: Fairer access for real fans
outcomes.text: Bot challenges and edge filtering reduce scalper purchases. Genuine concert-goers face less competition from automated scripts, which lowers complaint volume on social media.

outcomes.title: Faster issue response
outcomes.text: Tracing and centralized logs show where latency builds before fans notice. The operations team can act on slowdowns rather than reacting after complaints appear.

why.dns: Fans across Southeast Asia need to reach the ticketing site quickly. Managed DNS directs them to the nearest edge node without your team maintaining name servers.
why.esa: Concert images and seat maps slow page loads during a rush. Caching these assets at the edge reduces origin load, keeping the checkout flow responsive for fans buying K-pop tour tickets.
why.waf: Scalper bots flood the site during on-sales. Filtering known attack patterns at the edge reduces malicious traffic before it reaches your application, lowering the risk of another outage like last March.
why.alb: A thirty-fold traffic jump needs requests spread evenly. Distributing fans across two zones reduces the chance that one failure point takes the site down during a sale.
why.sae: Running idle servers between sales wastes money. Container-based compute scales from a small baseline to handle the rush and shrinks back, so you pay for capacity only when fans are buying.
why.tair: Two fans selecting the same seat causes double bookings. Holding temporary reservations in memory reduces conflicts and speeds up the checkout experience during high-demand on-sales.
why.polardb: Your team knows PostgreSQL well. A PostgreSQL-compatible managed database removes the effort of running your own cluster while keeping orders durable across two zones.
why.rocketmq: Last March the database was overwhelmed by sudden purchases. A queue holds each order until a worker saves it, reducing the risk of dropped transactions during the first ten minutes of a sale.
why.oss: Concert images and PDFs take up space on application servers. Storing media in object storage frees compute for ticket sales and lets the edge serve files directly.
why.arms: Slow pages frustrate fans before the team notices. Tracing latency across the purchase flow helps your staff find bottlenecks early, reducing complaints on social media.
why.sls: Troubleshooting after an incident takes time without central records. Collecting access and application logs in one place shortens investigations when something goes wrong during an on-sale.
why.cloud-backup: Losing order data would damage fan trust and revenue. Scheduled backups of the database and media files reduce the risk of permanent data loss.
why.captcha: Bots buy up seats for scalpers. Challenging suspicious users at login and checkout makes automated purchasing harder, giving real fans a fairer chance at tickets.

tradeoffs.text: Fans connect from across Southeast Asia while the application and database run in Singapore, adding network distance for some buyers.
tradeoffs.mitigation: Edge acceleration caches static content and optimizes dynamic routes to reduce perceived latency outside Singapore.

tradeoffs.text: The design assumes a peak load level; actual fan counts during a major K-pop tour may differ.
tradeoffs.mitigation: Run a load test matching your expected peak before the next on-sale to confirm scaling thresholds.

next: Approve a load test simulating your March on-sale traffic pattern to validate the design before the next major K-pop tour announcement.
